# Immutable Chunk Retrieval

**Content-addressed recovery of a compiled web client after HTML entry substitution, and hash pools that freeze the recovered tree.**

ItsNotAI LABS / KILN · 2026 · Working paper KILN-WP-10

## Abstract

A production JavaScript client is not a repository. It is a set of content-addressed files whose names already contain a hash, plus one HTML document that points at a single entry chunk. The HTML document is mutable. The hashed chunks, once published to a CDN that treats `/assets/*` as immutable, are not. Overwriting the document substitutes a different website while the previous website continues to exist as bytes behind the old hashes. This paper records the retrieval of KILN from that residue: the original entry `index-DkUKO55P.js`, the original store `store-sx46DNi5.js`, the original shell, Models, Studio, Explore, Marketplace, Wallet. It specifies hash pools — named ledgers of SHA-256 leaves with branched merkle roots — so the recovered tree cannot be lost again by a later entry substitution. Nothing in the original client is rewritten. New work is a new hash in a different pool or a new branch of an existing pool.

## 1. The object that was lost

KILN ships as a compiled TanStack Start client. The live document is a few hundred bytes. It loads one module:

    /assets/index-DkUKO55P.js

That module is the router, the document shell, and the importer of every other chunk. The filename is a content hash. Vite and Rollup emit it that way so a changed byte becomes a new URL. A CDN in front of `/assets/` with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` is allowed to keep that URL forever.

The product the user recognizes is not the HTML. It is the graph of chunks behind the entry:

- `AppShell-H-m5HQPd.js` — KILN · Git · L1, Models, Studio, Explore, Marketplace, Connect, Sign in
- `routes-BLZbLf8-.js` — homepage, "Let's build from here."
- `models-BywBH3wg.js` — Grok native, MEDINA, NeuroEmergence, XCREW, GPT, Claude, Gemini, Ollama
- `studio-fjyqp5G-.js` — one-shot a project, Conductor / Architect / Builder / Reviewer / Deployer
- `store-sx46DNi5.js` — 253,480 bytes of sealed-tree state, wallets, claims, papers
- `styles-A_fIl0Ci.css` — the original type and color
- `wallet-CTr0sTgn.js`, `explore-rtlBhl3C.js`, `marketplace-ZjEnaBK1.js`, `account-49nJUaQm.js`

When the HTML is rewritten to load a different entry — in this incident, `index-DuXWp-x1.js` — the visitor sees a different website. The old hashes remain. Retrieval is therefore a hash problem, not a source-control problem. The TypeScript that produced the chunks is gone. The chunks are not.

## 2. Failure mode: entry substitution

Call the document E and the entry chunk C. A compiled client is the pair (E → C) plus the transitive imports of C. E is small and is regenerated on every deploy. C is large and is named by its digest.

An overwrite of E that points at C′ is sufficient to hide C. It is not sufficient to delete C. Under an immutable asset policy, GET C continues to return 200 with the original bytes. GET of any hashed import of C likewise continues to return 200. What 404s are the chunks that were never on that CDN: lazy helpers that the original build expected but that a later deploy never uploaded, or that the CDN never cached because they were HTML fallbacks mistaken for JavaScript.

The observable of this incident:

1. The published HTML no longer referenced `index-DkUKO55P.js`.
2. `index-DkUKO55P.js` still answered 200.
3. `store-sx46DNi5.js` (253,480 bytes) still answered 200. The substitute store was 81 KB.
4. Original Models, Studio, AppShell, homepage chunks still answered 200.
5. Forty-six requested hashes returned the SPA HTML instead of JavaScript. Those hashes were never bytes on the CDN.

Retrieval is: collect every 200 that is actually JavaScript, reconstruct the missing hashes to the contract the entry already calls, and freeze the resulting tree by digest so a second overwrite of E cannot erase the set.

## 3. Retrieval procedure

The procedure is deterministic given a known entry hash.

### 3.1 Pin the entry

The original document named one module. That name is the pin:

    SHA-256(index-DkUKO55P.js) =
    0d2e955fc3c88b2aaa37eed414c12bf0a3a8048aa1bb7adca8b0a60b5cd5cb9e

The live copy of this file is 331,884 bytes. Two surgical edits exist relative to the 331,640-byte CDN copy: skip SSR hydration when `window.$_TSR` is absent, and fall back to `createRoot` when `hydrateRoot` would attach to an empty document. Those edits are classified `patched` in the freeze. They are not a rewrite of the product. They are the difference between a compiled SSR client and a static document that has no server-rendered markup.

### 3.2 Walk imports, keep only real JavaScript

For each `import` from the entry and from every subsequently reached chunk, GET the hashed URL. If the response is JavaScript, keep it. If the response is HTML, the hash was never a chunk; record it as missing. Do not treat an HTML fallback as a module. That is how a later site leaks into the original graph.

Ninety-three chunks in this freeze match the recovered `kiln-original` snapshot byte-for-byte (`cdn-original`). Two are patched, as above (`index-DkUKO55P.js`, `github-CPiTY5K-.js`). Forty-five are reconstructed.

### 3.3 Reconstruct missing hashes to a contract, not to a new product

The original entry imports `lazyRouteComponent-CtQWbmp_.js` as:

    { n as createFileRoute, r as createRootRoute, t as lazyRouteComponent }

`createRootRoute` is called as `pe({ beforeLoad, head, component })` and then `X._addFileChildren(...)`. A helper that returns a lazy-file-route factory will throw `X._addFileChildren is not a function`. A helper that sets both `id` and `path` on the root will fail TanStack `BaseRoute.init`: the root is not a root (`!options.path && !options.id` is false), `getParentRoute` is missing, production `invariant()` throws, the homepage is blank.

The reconstruction matches `@tanstack/router-core` `BaseRoute.init`:

1. `createFileRoute(path)` returns `(options) => Route(options)` and forces `isRoot = false`. It does not write `id` or `path` at construction. Those arrive later via `.update({ id, path, getParentRoute })`.
2. `createRootRoute(options)` does not set `id` or `path`. `init` therefore treats it as root, `_id = __root__`, `_path = "/"`.
3. Child `init` requires `getParentRoute()` to return an already-inited parent. The bundled `processRouteTree` inits parent before children.
4. Duplicate route ids call `invariant()` with no arguments during tree walk. Ids must be unique after join.

This is the only class of reconstruction this paper endorses: restore the contract the original entry already compiled against. Do not invent a second router. Do not invent a second homepage.

### 3.4 Static document, not a second SSR

The original root component renders `<html>`. The original boot calls `hydrateRoot(document, tree)`. An empty static document will mismatch. The retrieval serves the original `index.html` as a static file, stubs `/_serverFn/*` with `{ result: null }` so `beforeLoad` session does not throw `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'context')`, and lets the original client own the document. The product surfaces that come back are the original surfaces: home, Models, Studio, Explore, Marketplace, Wallet, Account, Start, papers.

### 3.5 Verify the product, not the toolchain

Retrieval is done when the document paints the original chrome and the original copy:

- Header: KILN · Git · L1 · Models · Studio · Explore · Marketplace
- Home: "The developer platform for the AI internet" / "Let's build from here."
- Models: native Grok, ItsNotAI LABS, bring-your-own
- Studio: one-shot a project, crew roles
- Wallet: one key, nested agent wallets

A green compiler is not verification. A GitHub-clone with Issues and Pulls as the landing surface is a different website.

## 4. Hash pools

A pool is a named ledger. A branch is a frozen snapshot inside a pool. A file is a SHA-256 object in `cas/sha256/<aa>/<hash>`. The HTML entry is never the source of truth. The merkle root of the pool branch is.

# Public Tree Import

**A same-origin engine that looks up any public GitHub account, pulls GitHub's own zipball, unpacks it, and seals every file into the connected wallet.**

ItsNotAI LABS / KILN · 2026 · Working paper KILN-WP-11

## Abstract

KILN import is not a curated gallery. The New surface already said so: paste a github.com URL, `owner/repo`, or a username / org; Kiln downloads the same archive GitHub builds under Code → Download ZIP; every file is sealed AES-256-GCM under the connected wallet; folder memory is indexed; a computer boots. That contract failed in production for two independent reasons. First, the compiled GitHub client treated a URL as `owner/repo` by splitting on the first slash, so `https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum` became owner `https:`. Second, unauthenticated `api.github.com` lookups hit the 60-request hourly quota and returned 403, so public accounts that the chips named — `ethereum`, `bitcoin`, `ItsNotAILABS`, `FreddyCreates` — painted "No public repositories found" even though the accounts were public. This paper records the engine that those buttons already call. The engine is same-origin. It looks up any public user or org. It searches when a token is not a login. It imports through zipball first and git tree second. Sealed trees land in the wallet that signed the import. Nothing in the original New page, Wallet, or store product graph is rewritten.

## 1. The object that is imported

A public GitHub repository is a named tree of blobs on a default branch. GitHub already publishes that tree three ways:

1. REST: `GET /users/{login}/repos`, `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}`, `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/trees/{sha}?recursive=1`
2. Zipball: `GET https://codeload.github.com/{owner}/{repo}/zip/refs/heads/{branch}` — the same bytes as Code → Download ZIP
3. Raw: `GET https://raw.githubusercontent.com/{owner}/{repo}/{branch}/{path}`

KILN's original New page (`new-DrGYWjdX.js`) already expected (2). The copy is explicit: "Kiln downloads GitHub's own zipball (the same archive as Code → Download ZIP), unpacks it, seals every file AES-256-GCM, indexes folder memory, and boots a computer." The list renderer already distinguishes `via === "zip"` from `"git tree"`. The zip inflater (`de`) already lives in that chunk. What was missing was an engine that actually performed the lookup against live GitHub instead of against a preloaded set, and that actually fetched the zipball instead of walking raw files one at a time until CORS or quota killed the loop.

The chips on that page — `ItsNotAILABS`, `FreddyCreates`, `ethereum`, `bitcoin`, `solana-labs`, `OpenZeppelin`, `Uniswap` — are queries, not a catalog. Clicking `ethereum` must list `ethereum/go-ethereum`, `ethereum/EIPs`, `ethereum/consensus-specs`. It must not fail because a previous hour of unauthenticated REST had spent the quota.

## 2. Failure modes

### 2.1 URL split

`githubListRepos` took `query.includes("/")` as the `owner/repo` signal and then `query.split("/")` as `[owner, repo]`. For a pasted URL:

    https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum
    split("/") → ["https:", "", "github.com", "ethereum", "go-ethereum"]
    owner = "https:"
    repo  = ""

GitHub 404. The user sees no repositories. The same function, given a login with no slash (`ethereum`), did the right thing *if and only if* REST was willing.

### 2.2 Unauthenticated quota

`api.github.com` allows 60 requests per hour per IP without a token. A page load that lists a user, then an org fallback, then a tree, then a commit, then raw files, spends that budget on one import. The next three public accounts return:

    API rate limit exceeded for 35.194.65.34.

The original compiled helper `github-CPiTY5K-.js` was a `createServerFn` stub. A later surgical patch called REST from the browser with no User-Agent and no fallback. Browser REST plus quota plus the URL bug is why "I looked up three different accounts and none of them were found" is the correct observation of a broken engine, not of missing accounts.

### 2.3 Zipball advertised, tree implemented

The New page logs `fetching GitHub zip for ${fullName}` and then calls `githubImportTree`. The patched helper fetched `git/trees?recursive=1` and then each blob from `raw.githubusercontent.com`. Large public trees (ethereum/go-ethereum) cannot be imported that way inside a browser hour. The advertised zipball was never requested.

### 2.4 Wallet as the landing

`importGithub` in the store refuses without a connected wallet. That is correct: a write is signed by a wallet, AES-256-GCM keys are HKDF-bound to `${walletSecret}:${repoId}`, the Merkle root settles as a `github_import` transaction. Lookup must still *list* without a wallet — the original UI already does — and Import must be the step that requires Connect. Ethereum-key import of the wallet itself is a different path: Connect → Import secret. A 64-char hex key, with or without `0x`, is the secret. The address is SHA-256 of that secret, not secp256k1. The chain id is Kiln L1 (747), not mainnet Ethereum. Pasting an Ethereum private key imports identity into Kiln; it does not replay mainnet state. Both paths were blocked when lookup returned empty, because the user never reached a tree to seal.

## 3. Engine

The engine is same-origin so the compiled client does not depend on CORS, User-Agent, or the GitHub REST quota.

    GET  /api/github/lookup?q=
    GET  /api/github/import?owner=&repo=

`githubListRepos` and `githubImportTree` — the two exports the original New page already imports — call those paths first. If the engine is down they fall back to `ungh.cc`, then REST, then search. The New page does not change.

### 3.1 Query grammar

A query is one of:

- a github.com URL, with or without `.git`, with or without `https://`
- `owner/repo`
- `@login` or `login` (user or org)
- a search string (spaces, or a token that is not a login)

URL parse is a single regular expression over `github.com[/:]([^/]+)(?:/([^/]+))?`. It is not `split("/")`.

### 3.2 Lookup order

For a login or org:

1. `GET https://ungh.cc/users/{login}/repos` — no GitHub REST quota, returns up to 100 public repositories
2. `GET api.github.com/users/{login}/repos` then `/orgs/{login}/repos`
3. HTML of `github.com/{login}?tab=repositories` and `github.com/orgs/{login}/repositories`, extracting `href="/{login}/{name}"`
4. GitHub search: `search/users?q=` then `search/repositories?q=`

For `owner/repo`: ungh repo, then REST repo. For a search string: search users (and list each of the first three), then search repositories. Results are deduped by `fullName`. Lookups cache five minutes so a chip click plus an Import does not spend the quota twice.

This is the same method used to retrieve the original compiled client: try the content-addressed host first, fall back to a slower host, never treat an HTML error page as the object.

### 3.3 Import order

1. Zipball. `codeload.github.com/{owner}/{repo}/zip/refs/heads/{branch}` (then `main`, `master`, `HEAD`). Cap 12 MiB. Unpack PKZIP local/central directory with raw DEFLATE (`zlib.inflateRaw`). Strip the GitHub-injected `{repo}-{branch}/` prefix. Drop directories named `node_modules`, `dist`, `.git`, and binary extensions. Drop files over 280 KiB or containing NUL in the first 800 bytes. Keep at most 180 text files and 6 MiB of UTF-8. This is the same cap the original New page's `de()` inflater already enforced on an uploaded `.zip`.
2. Git tree. `ungh.cc/repos/{owner}/{repo}/files/{branch}`, else REST `git/trees?recursive=1`. Fetch surviving blobs from `raw.githubusercontent.com`. Same caps.

`via` is `"zip"` or `"git tree"` so the original log line (`unpacked N files via GitHub zipball | git tree from SHA…`) paints the truth.

Huge repositories (go-ethereum at hundreds of megabytes) fail the zipball cap on purpose and fall through to the capped tree. The engine imports a working subset, not the whole history. That is honest. A 50 GB folder-memory deposit is a different paper (PXM, KILN-WP-01).

### 3.4 Seal into the wallet

The original `importGithub` action is unchanged:

1. Refuse if no wallet.
2. Refuse if the destination owner is not the wallet handle or an org the wallet

# The Kiln Account, Agentic Studio, and Live Computers

**A real handle (`kiln`) that owns every tech drop as a repository; a Studio whose crew, import, one-shot, computer, and CLI actually git-commit; and Merkle freeze of the recovered client after those surfaces came back.**

ItsNotAI LABS / KILN · 2026 · Working paper KILN-WP-12

## Abstract

KILN is not a GitHub clone with a copilot bolted on. A repository is a live computer. An agent that cannot write a file as a git commit is not an agent. A Fork button that is disabled until a wallet exists is a button that does not work. This paper records three closures on the recovered client: (1) the kiln account — a real in-app handle that publishes every sealed drop as `kiln/<name>`; (2) Studio restored as the tabbed agentic surface (Crew | Import | One-shot | Computer | CLI) whose tools settle `kiln_write_file` as Merkle commits; (3) GitHub import live on that Studio tab and as its own nav tab, sealing public trees — including the `reagent-systems/mouse` experiment — under the connected wallet. The pickup pin `recovered-20260903` stays immutable. This drop is a new hash-pool branch.

## 1. The kiln account

The forge needed an owner that is not a visitor's localStorage handle. Connecting without a name used to mint `itsnotailabs`. Tech drops then landed under whoever last clicked Connect. That is not an origin.

The kiln account is a user:

- handle `kiln`
- secret `kiln-operator-secret-v1-…` (16+ chars; address = SHA-256 of the secret)
- profile published at `/kiln-account.json`
- repositories `kiln/kiln`, `kiln/import-engine`, `kiln/hash-pool`, `kiln/mouse`, `kiln/studio`, plus one repo per freeze branch

Boot (`kiln-forge.js`) loads that document after zustand rehydrates, merges the trees into `userRepos`, and connects the kiln wallet only when no other wallet is present. It does not clobber a visitor who already connected. Fork, remix, branch, computer `write`, and agent `kiln_write_file` all require a wallet and an owner check. The kiln wallet satisfies both for every tree it owns. For every tree it does not own, the write path forks first, then commits.

This account is in-app. It is not a GitHub user named `kiln`. The public freeze record may also live under FreddyCreates / ItsNotAI LABS; that is a mirror, not the identity the buttons sign with.

## 2. Buttons that commit

The original chrome already had Fork, Remix, Branch. They were `disabled:!wallet`. A recovered client with skipHydration painted them dead until someone walked to Wallet, typed 16 characters, and came back.

The contract now:

1. Fork / Remix / Branch call `__KILN_ENSURE_WALLET` then mutate. They are never disabled for lack of a wallet.
2. `fork` copies the tree under `${wallet.handle}/${name}`, seals AES-256-GCM, settles a `fork` transaction, navigates to the new computer.
3. `remix` is a named fork (`${name}-remix`) with a `remix` transaction.
4. `branchFrom` forks if the wallet does not own the tree, then `createBranch`.
5. Computer `write <path> <body>` ensures a wallet, forks if needed, then `commitFile`. `commitFile` writes the blob, recomputes the Merkle root, appends a `merkle_commit` transaction, and records a git commit the log can print.
6. Agent tool `kiln_write_file` uses the same fork-for-write helper, then `commitFile`. The kernel POSTs `/api/kiln/agent-turn`; settlement is client-side. A file that did not commit is not a file.

The computer is not a log of pretend shell. `ls`, `cat`, `git status|log|branch`, `node`, `python`, `write` run against the sealed tree. Ports: capsule 443, MCP 7331, node 3000, python 8000, webgpu 7840.

## 3. Studio

The recovered Studio was a one-shot landing plus a crew list. The agentic Studio that belonged on this client had five tabs:

- **Crew** — spawn a role or a full crew (conductor, architect, builder, reviewer, deployer, scout, cipher, indexer). Each agent sits on a repo, reads the tree, and writes files as git commits. Default job: "Read the tree. Write the next real file as a git commit."
- **Import** — same GitHub zipball engine as New. Lookup any public user, org, or `owner/repo`. Import seals under the connected wallet and boots the computer.
- **One-shot** — prompt → complete tree including `index.html` → sealed capsule.
- **Computer** — kilnsh on the selected repo.
- **CLI** — `kiln ls|cat|write|run` via the same MCP tools agents use.

That surface is `studio-tabs.js`, mounted as the Studio route. Import also remains its own nav tab (`/new`), which is the original New page with the Import tab selected. Both call `githubListRepos` / `githubImportTree`. Both auto-connect the kiln wallet if none is present, so Import is not down because a button was disabled.

## 4. Mouse

`reagent-systems/mouse` is a public Swift tree (gesture-driven iOS/Android shell). The experiment is: fork it onto KILN and treat the tree as a live computer. Lookup of `reagent-systems/mouse` returns the zipball. Import seals it. The kiln account publishes a snapshot as `kiln/mouse` so the drop is a repository on the forge, not a URL on GitHub. A builder spawned on that computer writes the next file as a commit on `kiln/mouse` (or on the visitor's fork).

## 5. Wallet, on the landing

The homepage already said the platform was for developers and agents. It did not say how identity works. The recovered copy now does: connect a wallet — one key for you, nested wallets for every agent. A Connect wallet CTA lands on `/wallet`. The secret is ≥16 characters. The address is SHA-256 of that secret, Kiln L1 chain 747, not secp256k1, not mainnet Ethereum. Pasting an Ethereum key imports identity into Kiln; it does not replay mainnet state.

## 6. Merkle

Hash pools are named ledgers. Branches are frozen snapshots. Files live at `cas/sha256/<aa>/<hash>`. The pickup pin `recovered-20260903` cannot be overwritten. This paper's freeze is a new branch of pool `kiln-original`. The HTML entry still points at `index-DkUKO55P.js`. New work is reconstructed or patched chunks plus this markdown. A later overwrite of the document cannot erase the CAS objects.

    GET /freeze/HEAD.json
    GET /freeze/kiln-original--<branch>.json
    GET /kiln-account.json

Verify with the pool tool against the pin, then against HEAD.

## 7. What this is not

It is not a second website. It is not a GitHub user `kiln`. It is not a mocked agent. It is not a disabled Fork button. A write that does not produce a commit sha and a transaction hash did not happen.

# The Kiln Account as a Real Signer

**Fork, remix, and branch resolve to a new tree; the kiln wallet address is SHA-256 of `kiln-addr:<secret>`; computers execute node and python; agents git-commit.**

ItsNotAI LABS / KILN · 2026 · Working paper KILN-WP-13

## Abstract

A button that toasts "Forked" and stays on the origin is not a fork. The origin handle `kiln` forking `kiln/kiln` used to copy the id to `kiln/kiln-fork` while leaving `name: kiln`, so the chrome kept painting the origin and navigate landed on `/kiln/kiln`. This paper records the closure: a fork is a new `{id, name}` pair, the kiln account address is the same SHA-256 the wallet derives, every tech drop is a repository under `kiln/<name>`, the computer executes, and agents write files as commits.

## 1. The kiln account

Handle `kiln`. Secret `kiln-operator-secret-v1-…`. Address `SHA-256("kiln-addr:" + secret)` truncated to 20 bytes, hex, `0x`-prefixed — the same function `connect()` uses. 2. If this wallet already has a tree with `forkedFrom === source`, return it.

# The Git Tree as a Sealed Machine

**KILN treats every Git tree as its own sealed machine—shell, memory, models, preview domain, ledger.**

ItsNotAI LABS / KILN · 2026 · Working paper KILN-WP-14

## Abstract

A repository on a shared host is a folder with a URL. A repository on KILN is a machine. The computer page already said so. What it did not do, until this drop, is *seal* the five things a machine actually is so they cannot leak across trees: a shell with cwd, env, processes, and ports; memory in six banks; a bound model that agents inherit; a preview domain with an origin that is not the forge; a ledger that is the Merkle of this tree's commits and transactions, not the global chain. Isolation is the repo id. `kiln/kiln` cannot read `kiln/studio`'s banks, cannot share its blob origin, cannot bind a model onto it by accident. A button that opens a terminal on a shared box is not a computer. A Git tree that owns its shell, memory, models, preview domain, and ledger is.

## 1. The object

Call a Git tree T. T has an id `owner/name`, a working set of blobs, a Merkle root, a wallet that may write it. On KILN, T is also a machine M(T) with five facets:

1. **Shell** — kilnsh. cwd, env (`KILN_REPO`, `MODEL`, `DOMAIN`), processes (`init`, `kiln-agentd`, `kiln-memoryd`, `kiln-edged`, `kiln-indexerd`, `kiln-ledgerd`), ports (443 capsule, 7331 MCP, 3000 node, 8000 python, 7840 webgpu, 8443 sealed-cloud). Commands: `ls`, `cat`, `git`, `node`, `python`, `write`, `machine`, `model`, `memory`, `domain`, `ledger`, `seal`. A write is a git commit.
2. **Memory** — six banks scoped to T: working, episodic, semantic, procedural, lattice, folder. Folder memory is the inverted index of T's blobs plus Hilbert cells. The other banks are append-only records on M(T). Search never walks another tree.
3. **Models** — one bound model id on T (`repo.modelId`, written to `MACHINE.json`). Agents on T inherit it. Binding is `updateRepo` plus a commit. The org default is not T's model.
4. **Preview domain** — `owner-name.kiln.app` as the public host, and a blob: URL as the actual origin. The iframe sandbox is `allow-scripts allow-forms` without `allow-same-origin`, so the capsule cannot read the forge's storage. `window.Kiln` is injected with `{repo, isolation, model, domain, ledger}`. Relative assets rewrite to blob URLs from T's files only.
5. **Ledger** — Merkle of T's file root, T's commits, T's transactions. Printed by `ledger`. Not Kiln L1's global height. The global chain still settles `merkle_commit` / `capsule_boot` / `domain_bind`; the machine ledger is the slice that belongs to T, folded to a 20-byte hex root.

M(T) is persisted at `kiln-machines-v1` keyed by `owner/name`, and as `MACHINE.md` / `MACHINE.json` on the tree itself. Refreshing the tab does not mint a new computer. Opening a different tree does not reuse this one.

## 2. Failure modes

### 2.1 Shared box

An in-page Map of shells that dies on refresh is a demo. Two trees that share cwd or env are one machine with two names. The recovered computer stored shells in a module-level `Map` and never wrote them down. Isolation existed only for the lifetime of the tab.

### 2.2 Memory as grep

`memory search` walked T's files. That is folder memory, which is correct and stays. It is not working / episodic / semantic / procedural memory. Those kinds were named in the kernel constitution and never stored. A search on kiln/kiln could not be proven not to include kiln/studio's mailbox because mailboxes were a global agent list filtered after the fact.

### 2.3 Global model

The Models page has Assign. Spawn already fell back to `repo.modelId`. Nothing *bound* the model onto the tree as a constitution, so a visitor who never opened Models ran Grok-4.6 on every computer, including ones that had a different id painted in About. Binding was a UI preference, not a facet of the machine.

### 2.4 Parent-origin preview

The preview iframe used a `data:` URL with `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms allow-same-origin"`. A data URL is opaque, but `allow-same-origin` plus a later `blob:` would collapse to the forge origin. Relative assets did not load. `window.Kiln` was not bound. The host `owner-name.kiln.app` was a string in chrome, not an origin the capsule ran on.

### 2.5 Global ledger

Commits and txs already carried `repoId`. The computer never printed the slice. Merkle on About was the file tree. A machine ledger is the fold of files + commits + txs for T. Without it, "this tree's history" was a filter on a global log.

## 3. Closure

The kernel is `machine-seal.js`. Boot (`kiln-forge.js`) seals every origin tree the kiln account publishes, writes `MACHINE.md` if missing, remembers an episodic boot, ensures the kiln.app domain, seats builder + conductor.

```

GET  /kiln/kiln/preview      isolated blob origin

     / % ledger

```

`seal` is the isolation proof: count of sealed machines, this tree's cwd / banks / bound model / host / ledger root, and a cross-check that no working-bank id, env.KILN_REPO, or domain host is shared with another tree.

`model <id>` calls `bindModel`: `updateRepo({modelId})`, persist M(T), remember procedural, `commitFile MACHINE.json`. Agents spawned after that inherit `repo.modelId` (the store already did). Agents running now see it on the next kernel turn (`agent.modelId || repo.modelId || default`).

The MCP tools `kiln_machine`, `kiln_bind_model`, `kiln_remember`, `kiln_ledger` dispatch into the same kernel. `kiln_run` already executed kilnsh; it now understands the new commands because they live in `runOnMachine`.

It is not a VM. It is not a Docker container. It is not a Cloudflare isolate. It is a Git tree that owns five facets and can prove they do not leak. Node and Python still execute on the host via `/api/kiln/run` with a tempdir per invocation — that is process isolation for a command, not the machine. # kiln/infra

Python infrastructure models. Merkle, lock, machine, capsule, physics. Callable as kiln_* tools during a build.

# Laws

1. Hash conservation. Same bytes, same SHA-256.
2. Odd merkle leaf is duplicated.
3. A write moves the root.
4. Isolation is the repo id. Blob origins do not cross trees.
5. Preview is isolatePreview — unique origin, sandbox allow-scripts allow-forms.

"""Platform physics. Conservation laws the kiln actually obeys.

These are not metaphors. They are checks an agent can run on a tree
during a build. Failures are real: hash drift, isolation leak, merkle
mismatch.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from .machine import host_of, isolation_of, seal
from .merkle import merkle_hex, merkle_of_files, sha256_hex


def law_hash_conservation(body: str | bytes = b"kiln") -> dict:
    a = sha256_hex(body)
    b = sha256_hex(body)
    return {"law": "hash-conservation", "ok": a == b, "digest": a}


def law_merkle_odd_leaf() -> dict:
    three = [sha256_hex(b"a"), sha256_hex(b"b"), sha256_hex(b"c")]
    four = [sha256_hex(b"a"), sha256_hex(b"b"), sha256_hex(b"c"), sha256_hex(b"c")]
    # Odd layer duplicates the last leaf. Three leaves == four with last repeated.
    return {
        "law": "merkle-odd-leaf",
        "ok": merkle_hex(three) == merkle_hex(four),
        "root": merkle_hex(three),
    }


def law_write_changes_root(files: list[dict]) -> dict:
    before = merkle_of_files(files)
    extra = list(files) + [{"path": "__kiln_probe__", "content": "probe"}]
    after = merkle_of_files(extra)
    ok = (not files and after["root"] != before["root"]) or after["root"] != before["root"]
    return {
        "law": "write-conservation",
        "ok": ok,
        "before": before["root"],
        "after": after["root"],
    }


def law_isolation(repo_a: str, repo_b: str) -> dict:
    if repo_a == repo_b:
        return {"law": "isolation", "ok": False, "error": "need two distinct repo ids"}
    a = isolation_of(repo_a)
    b = isolation_of(repo_b)
    ha = host_of(repo_a)
    hb = host_of(repo_b)
    return {
        "law": "isolation",
        "ok": a != b and ha != hb,
        "a": {"repo": repo_a, "isolation": a, "host": ha},
        "b": {"repo": repo_b, "isolation": b, "host": hb},
    }


def check_tree(repo: dict, other: dict | None = None) -> dict:
    machine = seal(repo)
    laws = [
        law_hash_conservation(),
        law_merkle_odd_leaf(),
        law_write_changes_root(repo.get("files") or []),
    ]
    if other and other.get("id") and other["id"] != repo.get("id"):
        laws.append(law_isolation(repo["id"], other["id"]))
    elif repo.get("id"):
        other_id = "kiln/other" if repo["id"] != "kiln/other" else "kiln/studio"
        laws.append(law_isolation(repo["id"], other_id))
    failed = [x for x in laws if not x.get("ok")]
    return {
        "ok": not failed,
        "repo": repo.get("id"),
        "isolation": machine["isolation"],
        "host": machine["domain"]["host"],
        "merkle": machine["ledger"]["merkle"],
        "laws": laws,
        "failed": [x["law"] for x in failed],
    }

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""JSON tool dispatcher. Stdin: {tool, args}. Stdout: result.

Grok and the crew call these as kiln_* tools during a build.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from .capsule import assemble
from .lock import inspect, load_lock, summary
from .machine import seal
from .merkle import merkle_of_files
from .physics import check_tree
from .repos import find_repo

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]


def _repo(args: dict) -> dict:
    repo_id = args.get("repo") or args.get("repoId") or "kiln/studio"
    files = args.get("files")
    return find_repo(ROOT, str(repo_id), files)


def kiln_merkle(args: dict) -> dict:
    repo = _repo(args)
    tree = merkle_of_files(repo.get("files") or [])
    tree["ok"] = True
    tree["repo"] = repo.get("id")
    tree["text"] = f"{repo.get('id')} merkle {tree['root']} · {tree['files']} files · {tree['bytes']}B"
    return tree


def kiln_lock(args: dict) -> dict:
    lock = load_lock(ROOT)
    rows = inspect(ROOT, lock)
    out = summary(rows)
    out["spec"] = lock.get("spec")
    out["sourceBranch"] = lock.get("sourceBranch")
    out["text"] = out["text"]
    return out


def kiln_machine(args: dict) -> dict:
    repo = _repo(args)
    machine = seal(repo)
    machine["ok"] = True
    machine["text"] = (
        f"{machine['repoId']}\n"
        f"isolation {machine['isolation']}\n"
        f"cipher {machine['cipher']}\n"
        f"model {machine['models']['bound']}\n"
        f"domain {machine['domain']['host']}\n"
        f"ledger {machine['ledger']['root']}\n"
        f"merkle {machine['ledger']['merkle']}"
    )
    return machine


def kiln_capsule(args: dict) -> dict:
    repo = _repo(args)
    cap = assemble(repo)
    html = cap.pop("html")
    include = bool(args.get("html"))
    cap["ok"] = True
    cap["bytes"] = len(html.encode("utf-8"))
    if include:
        cap["html"] = html
    cap["text"] = (
        f"capsule {cap['repo']} · {cap['host']} · entry {cap['entry']}\n"
        f"isolation {cap['isolation']}\n"
        f"merkle {cap['merkle']}\n"
        f"sandbox {cap['sandbox']}"
    )
    return cap


def kiln_preview(args: dict) -> dict:
    cap = kiln_capsule({**args, "html": False})
    cap["preview"] = f"/{cap['repo']}/preview"
    cap["text"] = cap["text"] + f"\npreview {cap['preview']}"
    return cap


def kiln_physics(args: dict) -> dict:
    repo = _repo(args)
    other_id = args.get("other")
    other = find_repo(ROOT, str(other_id), None) if other_id else None
    out = check_tree(repo, other)
    failed = out.get("failed") or []
    out["text"] = (
        f"physics {out.get('repo')} {'ok' if out.get('ok') else 'FAIL ' + ','.join(failed)}\n"
        f"isolation {out.get('isolation')}\n"
        f"host {out.get('host')}\n"
        f"merkle {out.get('merkle')}\n"
        + "\n".join(f"{x['law']} {'ok' if x.get('ok') else 'FAIL'}" for x in out.get("laws") or [])
    )
    return out


def kiln_infra(args: dict) -> dict:
    model = str(args.get("model") or args.get("name") or "physics").strip()
    inner = {k: v for k, v in args.items() if k not in ("model", "name")}
    return dispatch("kiln_" + model if not model.startswith("kiln_") else model, inner)


DISPATCH = {
    "kiln_merkle": kiln_merkle,
    "kiln_lock": kiln_lock,
    "kiln_machine": kiln_machine,
    "kiln_capsule": kiln_capsule,
    "kiln_preview": kiln_preview,
    "kiln_physics": kiln_physics,
    "kiln_infra": kiln_infra,
}


def dispatch(name: str, args: dict | None = None) -> dict:
    args = args or {}
    fn = DISPATCH.get(name)
    if not fn:
        return {"ok": False, "error": f"unknown infra model {name}", "text": f"unknown infra model {name}"}
    try:
        return fn(args)
    except Exception as e:
        return {"ok": False, "error": str(e), "text": str(e)}


def main() -> int:
    raw = sys.stdin.read()
    if not raw.strip():
        raw = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "{}"
    try:
        req = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        json.dump({"ok": False, "error": f"invalid json: {e}", "text": f"invalid json: {e}"}, sys.stdout)
        return 1
    if isinstance(req, str):
        req = json.loads(req)
    tool = req.get("tool") or req.get("name") or req.get("model") or "kiln_physics"
    args = req.get("args") or req.get("arguments") or req
    if isinstance(args, dict) and args is req:
        args = {k: v for k, v in req.items() if k not in ("tool", "name")}
    out = dispatch(str(tool), args if isinstance(args, dict) else {})
    json.dump(out, sys.stdout)
    sys.stdout.write("\n")
    return 0 if out.get("ok", True) else 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

`swift/project.yml`. There is no test target; verification is running the

changes verify headlessly: compile with a scratch `main.swift` of assertions

engine wrote; the packfile writer must pass `git index-pack --stdin`; the

upload-pack --stateless-rpc` with the ACK/NAK preamble demuxed and haves
honored (incremental pack smaller than the full closure); and the merge
engine must match `git merge-file` on the line merge (clean + conflict
cases) and a real repo on the FF/three-way outcomes (`fsck` clean, both
parents present, byte-identical content).

never be checked — a JSValue travelling to the JS thread, where it is only ever
called. Keep the build WARNING-FREE; these are errors under the Swift 6 language
mode.
Pack inflate uses **libz** (`-lz` in project.yml), not the Compression
framework, which can't delimit concatenated zlib members.
`TerminalScreen.swift` and `TerminalPrograms.swift` are also
app-independent: verify the screen against xterm semantics AND cross-check
against a known-good emulator (`pip install pyte`; feed both the same
escape streams — structured + seeded-random — and diff final screen text;
pyte needs two harness-side patches: materialize its sparse buffer rows
before IL/DL, and clamp CUU/CUD at margins only when the cursor starts
inside the region). Programs verify by wiring `TerminalProgramIO.write`
into an `AnsiParser` and asserting the grid after keystrokes.

deliberately xterm-faithful — bare LF is *index* (cursor down, same
column), matching pyte. A real PTY maps NL→CR-NL on output, so ink-style

## [1.4] - 2026-08-12

### Fixed
- iOS: **`npm run dev` works.** A SvelteKit project on the phone starts its dev server once
  and serves the rendered page. Five faults sat on top of each other:
  - The project was rooted at `/`, and chokidar records a directory under its parent — for
    `/`, POSIX gives dirname `/` and basename `""`, so it filed an empty-named child in the
    root's own record, decided on the next read that it had been deleted, and tore the whole
    tree down. Every file was reported `unlink`ed, `vite.config.ts` among them, so vite
    restarted about every three seconds. A program now starts at a named root.
  - ESM named imports were a snapshot rather than a live binding, so a module exporting
    `let x` and assigning it later read `undefined` forever. Svelte's compiler then ran half
    in dev mode and every page died inside svelte's own renderer.
  - `Request`/`Response` bodies built from a `Uint8Array` went through `String(body)`, so a
    rendered page arrived as comma-separated character codes.
  - `listen()` with no host bound IPv4-only where node binds dual-stack, so a program could
    not reach its own server by name.
  - "Failed to run dependency scan" was downstream of the restart storm, not a second bug.
- iOS: **the commit graph shows the whole history.** It stopped four times over: one
  80-commit API page with no second request, a 200-commit cap per branch, an unreadable
  ancestor discarding that branch's history entirely, and a reader that could not see
  anything packed — neither objects in a packfile nor refs in `packed-refs`, and not
  branch names containing a slash, which live in a directory. On this repository that was
  310 commits and 11 branches where git counts 423 and 21. Reading it all is also now
  faster than reading part of it was.
- iOS: **the terminal's key strip no longer dismisses the keyboard.** `up`, `down`, `esc`
  and the rest are registered hold regions, so a TUI keeps the keyboard while you drive it.

### Added
- iOS: **tapping a project's name in the Files container goes back to the picker.** Leaving
  stops whatever the ring's terminal was running — outright, not with a `^C` a dev server
  would read as a keystroke and ignore — so no server keeps a port after its project is gone.
- **Tailwind 3 compiles on the phone**, via the wasm build of lightningcss. Tailwind 4
  cannot: `@tailwindcss/oxide`'s wasi build declares shared memory, and JSC will not parse
  such a module while `useSharedArrayBuffer` is restricted in Apple's build.
- Five gates for behaviour that had none — `watchroot`, `stackshape`, `lightningcss`,
  `tailwind`, `leaveproject` — and `githistory`, which holds the commit graph against real
  git's own answer on a repository whose objects and refs are both packed.

# compile.md — running and compiling code on the device

The question underneath the `system` work, asked for every language at once:

> *What can Mouse compile and run on the phone itself, with no machine on
> the other end?*

**Verdict: more than expected, and the ordering is counter-intuitive.**
Web languages reach *full native speed today* through a door most people
miss. C and C++ compile on device for real. Systems languages with
LLVM-sized compilers stay on CI. Nothing here needs an entitlement Apple
withholds.

This is a plan, not shipped behavior. Two companions:
**[system.md](system.md)** is the umbrella spec (platform physics, the
runtime substrate, Mouse-as-kernel, the **Node compatibility layer** that
makes `npx` reachable, and the unified phase map);
**[xcode.md](xcode.md)** covers the one case this document defers — signing
and installing a native iOS app.

## 1. The two questions

Every language splits into two independent questions, and conflating them
is what makes this topic confusing:

1. **Can the compiler run here?** A compiler is just a program. It needs to
   be native (built into Mouse), interpreted, or wasm.
2. **Can the output run here?** Also just a program. Same three answers.

A language has a **full on-device loop** only when both are yes. When only
the second is yes, the loop routes compilation through CI and runs the
artifact here — which is still a real workflow, not a consolation prize.

## 2. The four execution substrates

Everything in this document runs on one of four surfaces. Their speeds
differ by more than an order of magnitude, so choosing correctly per
workload *is* the architecture.

| Substrate | Speed | Runs what | Constraint |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Native (in-app)** | 1× | Swift, and any C/C++ library compiled in at build time | Roster fixed at ship time; app-size cost |
| **WKWebView** | ~1–3× | JS and wasm, **JIT-compiled** | Web APIs only; needs a visible view; no direct filesystem |
| **In-app wasm runtime** | ~5–30× | Any `.wasm` | Interpreted; we write it |
| **In-app JavaScriptCore** | ~10–30× | JS | **Interpreter only — see below** |

### The JIT nuance that reorders everything

There is exactly one legal JIT on iOS: **WebKit's**. The web content
process carries a code-signing entitlement third-party apps cannot get, and
Apple grants it to the browser engine any app may embed.

The consequence is sharp, and Mouse is currently on the wrong side of it:

- `JSContext` **in our process has no JIT.** It runs WebKit's low-level
  interpreter. This is the `js` engine in [Terminal.swift](swift/Mouse/Terminal.swift)

# Contributing to Mouse

Thanks for wanting to work on this. Mouse is small, opinionated, and moving
fast — this document is what you need to be productive without stepping on
the things that make it work.

## Setup

Two native apps; build the one you're touching (full build/run instructions,
including the simulator and emulator, are in the [README](README.md)).

**iOS (`swift/`)** — macOS + **Xcode 16+** + `brew install xcodegen`:

```sh
cd swift && xcodegen generate && open Mouse.xcodeproj
```

`Mouse.xcodeproj` is **generated** from [swift/project.yml](swift/project.yml).
Never hand-edit the project file; change `project.yml` and re-run
`xcodegen generate`. Re-run it whenever you add, remove, or rename a source
file. The regenerated `.xcodeproj` is committed, so include it in your PR if
it changed.

**Android (`kotlin/`)** — **JDK 21** + the Android SDK (open `kotlin/` in
Android Studio, or `./gradlew assembleDebug`). No generated project file.

The two apps share no code — a feature added to one should be mirrored in the
other (or the PR should say why not). Parity is by faithful re-implementation
(`Shell.swift` ↔ `MouseShell.kt`, `CarouselDeck.swift` ↔ `Model.kt`, …).

## Ground rules

- **The gesture law is architecture, not preference.** One-finger horizontal
  drags and all two-finger gestures belong to the shell, everywhere; content
  gets taps, vertical scrolling, and the keyboard (and while an editor is
  focused, drags on it belong to the text). Any input-handling change must
  say, in the PR description, how it upholds the law.
- **Zero dependencies is a feature.** The app ships with no third-party code
  — even tar/gzip extraction is hand-written against the platform. Adding a
  dependency needs a discussion issue first, with the "what would it take to
  not add it" answer written down. (Planned exceptions live on the
  [roadmap](ROADMAP.md): libgit2, esbuild, Runestone.)
- **Experiment freely; merge carefully.** Spike on branches, keep whole
  experimental directions alive as `*-experiments` branches, use whatever
  throwaway UI and diagnostics help you explore. The bar lives at `main`:
  what merges is feel-tested on a real device, and it lands clean — no
  leftover demo scaffolding or diagnostic code.
- **Comments state constraints, not narration.** The codebase leans on
  comments that explain *why the obvious alternative fails* (there are
  several load-bearing ones — see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for the map).
  Match that: no "this line does X" comments, no change-log comments.
- **Docs move with behavior.** If your change alters what a gesture does or
  what a container can do, update [swift/README.md](swift/README.md)
  (Gestures / Functionality sections). If it changes how things look or move,
  update [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md).

## Verifying changes

There is no test target yet (unit tests for the pure cores — tar/gzip, graph
layout — are welcome). Merging to `main` means the change was tested for
**function and feel**:

1. Build clean — iOS: `xcodebuild -project swift/Mouse.xcodeproj -scheme
   Mouse -destination 'generic/platform=iOS Simulator' build`; Android:
   `cd kotlin && ./gradlew assembleDebug`. Build the platform(s) you touched.
2. Exercise what you touched **plus the gesture matrix near it**: lane
   swipe, edge swipe, divider drag, pinch, and — if you were near the
   editor — tap-to-focus, selection drag, tap-outside dismiss.
3. **Feel it on a real device.** Gesture latency, spring weight, keyboard
   behavior, and performance are the product; the simulator can't vouch for
   them (and lies about CPU with the keyboard up — see
   [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md)). If it feels worse, it isn't done, even if it
   works.
4. Force-quit and relaunch: the strip must restore (persistence breaks are
   easy to miss and painful to bisect).

CI builds every push and PR; a red build blocks review.

# Mouse — Design Language

The source of truth for how Mouse looks, moves, and speaks. The interaction
model itself (rings, lanes, the gesture law) is specified in
[swift/README.md](swift/README.md); this document is about everything you
see and feel.

## 1. Principles

- **Mobile-first, one-handed or two handed.** Designed for a phone held in one hand;
  every control reachable, every gesture performable with a thumb. iPad is
  a bigger window, not a different app. With two hands you can type easier, but it would be cool to add voice controlled UI for accessibility. "Go to this project" or "Run this command in the terminal for me." are some examples.
- **Motion is the arrow.** Nothing points, pulses a tutorial overlay, or
  draws a coach mark. When the UI wants to teach a gesture, it *performs a
  hint of the gesture*: the swipe lesson nudges sideways, the pinch lesson
  breathes smaller. Idle animations are the entire onboarding vocabulary.
- **Terminal honesty.** The visual language is a terminal's: monospace
  everything, black panels, text that states facts. Errors say what
  happened and why — never "something went wrong", never reassurance copy.
- **The container is the chrome.** No toolbars, no tab bars, no navigation
  stacks. Every capability lives inside a container or on its surface
  (corner chips), and the shell's gestures are the only navigation.
- **Calm, physical motion.** Springs everywhere, sized to feel like the
  surfaces have mass. Nothing teleports; things that leave slide or settle. We shouldn't have any flickering, or any lag that causes jitter-like motion. 

## 2. Surfaces

| Token | Value | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Canvas | pure white | The app background |
| Backdrop art | near-white tints `#F4F6FA` / `#FAF5F6` | The ASCII logo behind everything (static; its animation is intentionally off — it costs a frame loop) |
| Container | pure black, corner radius **32 pt continuous** | Every real container |
| Lesson container | black with a `white @ 0.35` 1 pt inner stroke | Onboarding presets — outlined reads as instructional, filled reads as content |
| Side gutters | **24 pt** | Between containers and screen edges (widens to 40 pt during the edge lesson) |
| Container padding | **16 pt** | Content inset inside a container |
| Divider gap | **32 pt** tall, capsule handle 40 × 5 `secondary @ 0.45` | Between lanes; grows to 48 pt when a lesson word needs the gap |

Depth comes from geometry (black on white, big radii), never from shadows,
blurs, or gradients on surfaces.

## 3. Type

One family: **IBM Plex Mono Bold** (`AppFont.asciiName`), everywhere — UI,
editor, terminal, lesson words. No second typeface, no weights ladder.

| Size | Role |
|---|---|
| 28 | Lesson words ("Swipe?", "Edge Swipe?") — uniform across all lessons |
| 14 | Empty-state prompts |
| 13 | Body text in containers (graph rows, notes) |
| 12 | Editor text, terminal |
| 11 | Metadata (container headers like `owner/repo — history`) |

Line height is 1.2× fixed (`asciiParagraphStyle`). Editor and terminal text
**wraps** — horizontal panning belongs to the shell, so content never wants
it.

## 4. Color

Mouse is monochrome with one sanctioned exception.

- Text on black: white at **1.0** (content), **0.85** (secondary content),
  **0.6 / 0.55** (metadata, prompts, disabled).
- Text on white (lesson words outside containers): pure black.
- **The exception:** the commit graph's branch rails cycle an 8-color
  palette (orange, pink, cyan, green, purple, yellow, blue, red) — data
  encoding, not decoration.
- Red marks failure states (a failed sync in the git toolbar). Nothing else
  is colored. There is no accent color; if a design wants one, the design
  isn't finished.

# Mouse for Android

The native Android app, in Kotlin + Jetpack Compose. Same product, same
design language ([DESIGN.md](../DESIGN.md)), same interaction spec as the
Swift app ([swift/README.md](../swift/README.md)) — built natively for its
platform, per the no-cross-platform-frameworks rule.

## Building

Requirements: **JDK 21** and the **Android SDK** (Android Studio installs both).

Android Studio: open this `kotlin/` folder. CLI:

```sh
cd kotlin
./gradlew assembleDebug
```

On macOS, if Gradle can't find the SDK:

```sh
ANDROID_HOME=~/Library/Android/sdk ./gradlew assembleDebug
```

Toolchain: Gradle 8.14, AGP 8.10, Kotlin 2.0, Compose (BOM 2024.09),
minSdk 26 / target 35. Zero third-party libraries beyond the platform +
Compose + coroutines — even tar/gzip (`GZIPInputStream` + a hand-written tar
reader), JSON (`org.json`), HTTP (`HttpURLConnection`), and checksums
(`MessageDigest`) are the SDK's own.

## Running on an emulator

### Android Studio (easiest)

1. Install [Android Studio](https://developer.android.com/studio).
2. **File → Open** → select this `kotlin/` folder (not the repo root).
3. **Tools → Device Manager → Create Device** — pick a phone (e.g. Pixel 9)
   and a recent system image (API 35 or similar). Start the virtual device.
4. Click **Run** (green play button). Android Studio builds, installs, and

# Android parity: everything the iOS app can do

The Kotlin app (`kotlin/`, ~2,600 lines) is a real parity app for the
carousel, workspaces, git, GitHub and a from-scratch `msh` — but phases
**T** (terminal screen), **F** (package manager) and **G** (the Node layer)
are iOS-only by a decision recorded in AGENTS.md. This plan triggers that
decision deliberately, on the user's instruction, and says which path it
takes and why.

## What Android actually permits

The premise that started this — "Android isn't stuck by the JIT problem" —
is half right, and the half that is wrong decides the architecture.

**Free on Android, blocked on iOS:**
- **JIT.** No page-level code-signing enforcement. A WebView JITs
  JavaScript. The interpreted-speed ceiling that shapes the whole iOS
  engine simply is not there.
- **Process creation.** `fork`/`exec` work. The app already ships an `sh`
  engine that runs `/system/bin/sh`, which iOS can never do.

**Blocked on Android too, for a different reason:**
- **Executing downloaded binaries.** Since API 29, an app targeting 29+
  cannot exec a file from its own writable data directory — SELinux
  refuses. This app targets SDK 35. So the Termux model ("`pkg install`
  fetches real ARM binaries and runs them") is NOT available without either
  dropping targetSdk (Play Store will not accept it; this is why Termux
  distributes on F-Droid) or shipping the binaries inside the APK.

**The one genuine Android unlock:** binaries in the APK's native-library
directory ARE executable. A real `node` could ship that way.

## The three paths, and the choice

**A — bundle real binaries in the APK.** Ship node (and later python) as
native libs. No engine to write; real V8 with JIT. Costs: the runtime set
is frozen at build time, every update needs a release, and the APK carries
every runtime whether or not a user wants it. This is the thing the iOS
side deliberately rejected ("runtimes are installed as data, never
bundled") and it forfeits the property the user has asked for most
consistently: install whatever you need.

**B — port the engine into a WebView. ← recommended, and what this plan
does.** The Node engine's JS bootstrap is ~72 % portable (measured, per
system.md); the host bridge is the 28 % that gets rewritten in Kotlin
against `@JavascriptInterface`. Runtimes stay wasm, downloaded — so the
exec restriction never applies, and `swift/Runtimes.json` is reused
verbatim because the catalog is data. JIT comes free from the WebView, so
Android gets the same capability as iOS and is faster at it.

**C — Termux model, sideload only.** Most capable; gives up the Play Store.
Only worth it if distribution is F-Droid/APK anyway.

**Open question for the user, and the only thing that would change this
plan: does the Android app need to stay Play-Store-shippable?** If no, C
becomes worth costing. Everything in Milestones 1–3 below is common to all
three paths, so this plan starts without the answer.

## Milestones

Each ends in a commit with evidence, and nothing counts until it runs on an
emulator (AVDs present: `Pixel_9`, `Medium_Phone_API_36.0`, `Medium_Tablet`;
SDK at `~/Library/Android/sdk`, JDK 21; nothing is on PATH — export

**2 — Phase F: the package manager.** Port `PackageManager.swift`: npm
registry, semver, integrity, lockfiles, `npm run`/`npx`. Kotlin already has

# Releasing Mouse

Releases are cut from **`main`** by pushing a version tag. A GitHub Action
([`.github/workflows/release.yml`](.github/workflows/release.yml)) then builds
both apps and publishes a GitHub Release with the artifacts attached and
generated notes.

## Versioning

SemVer (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`). Keep the two apps' versions in step:

- **iOS**: `MARKETING_VERSION` in [swift/project.yml](swift/project.yml)
  (re-run `xcodegen generate` after changing it).
- **Android**: `versionName` (and bump `versionCode` by 1) in
  [kotlin/app/build.gradle.kts](kotlin/app/build.gradle.kts).

## Cutting a release

1. Land everything for the release on `main` and make sure CI is green.
2. Bump the versions above and move the `## [Unreleased]` block in
   [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) to `## [x.y.z] - YYYY-MM-DD`, then start a
   fresh `## [Unreleased]`.
3. Commit, then tag and push:
   ```sh
   git tag v0.2.0
   git push origin main v0.2.0
   ```
4. The **Release** workflow runs, builds the Android APK and the iOS
   simulator app, and publishes a GitHub Release with generated notes and
   both artifacts attached.
5. Edit the published release to paste in the changelog highlights.

You can also trigger it from the Actions tab (**Release → Run workflow**)
with a tag name, without pushing a tag.

## What ships in a release

| Asset | What it is | Who it's for |
|---|---|---|
| `mouse-android-vX.Y.Z.apk` | Debug-signed APK | Sideload on any device (`adb install`) or an emulator |
| `mouse-ios-sim-vX.Y.Z.zip` | Simulator `.app` | Reviewers running it in the iOS Simulator without Xcode |

A `mouse-ios-vX.Y.Z.ipa` ships beside those: the `ios-ipa` job signs a device
build with the repository's Apple secrets —

- `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_P12` + `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` (the Distribution cert)
- `APPLE_PROVISIONING_PROFILE` (an App Store profile for the bundle id)
- `APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY` + `APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_ID` + `APP_STORE_CONNECT_ISSUER_ID`

Signing is manual and pinned to the uploaded profile: its plist supplies the
name, UUID and team at run time, so rotating a secret rotates the signing with
no workflow change. Every run VALIDATES the package against App Store Connect;
only a real tag push UPLOADS to TestFlight — a `workflow_dispatch` rehearsal
proves the whole path without publishing a build. Validation and upload need
the app record to exist in App Store Connect for the bundle id; until it does,
the validate step fails naming exactly that.

The certificate expires yearly. When the archive step starts failing with a
signing error, re-export the cert and replace `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_P12` — nothing
else changes.

# Roadmap

Mouse's vision is bigger than an IDE: it's a gesture shell that absorbs the
jobs of whole desktop products, one product at a time. Each absorption is a
**product branch** — a long-running branch that asks one question:

> *What would X be if it had been born on a phone?*

A product branch is an exploration space: it can carry demo scaffolding,
half-ideas, and dead ends. Slices graduate to `main` when they're feel-tested
and clean (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)). Branches spawn when work
starts, not before — this page is the map of intended branches, in rough
order of attack.

## Platform stance

**Native per platform, no bridges.** Two apps sharing one spec and one
design language: `swift/` (iOS/iPadOS, the lead platform) and `kotlin/`
(Android, at feature parity — same shell, GitHub, workspaces, containers).
No web builds and no cross-platform
frameworks — the earlier Capacitor/web incarnation was removed deliberately
and is not coming back. Each platform gets the gesture shell built against
its own touch system, done properly — and each keeps its honest advantages
(Android apps may run the system shell; iOS gets the from-scratch `msh`).

## Product branches

### `vs-code` — the editor *(active today as `vs-code-features`)*

The IDE absorption: workspaces, file tree, in-place editor, commit graph,
terminal, push/pull. Largely shipped (see below). Still on this branch's
plate:

- **Git, merges**: the local engine, the remote half, AND native merges are
  BUILT (`GitCore` + `GitRemote`: clone/fetch/push over smart-HTTP, packfiles
  with delta resolution, push that auto-creates the GitHub repo via
  `POST /user/repos`, and a three-way merge engine — fast-forward /
  merge-commit / diff3 conflict markers — verified against `git merge-file`
  and a real repo). The git module toolbar (`commit · sync · branch · merge
  · refresh` in the Graph header) drives them; `sync` pushes, and pulling is
  the explicit `git pull` in the terminal (incremental fetch into the
  tracking ref + native merge — the app never rewrites a user's files on
  its own). Remaining: a `git clone` entry in the project picker
- Editor upgrades: syntax highlighting + line numbers (Runestone/TextKit 2),
  find in file, font-size setting, large-file strategy
- ~~Terminal engines~~ **Shipped** (phases F/G/D — see STATUS.md): the
  package engine (`npm`/`pnpm install` from the real registry, lockfiles,
  integrity, native-binary→wasm substitution) and the dev-server engine
  (vite/esbuild through the Node layer, HMR, serving clients outside the
  app). Remaining: a Preview container — an in-app surface for what the
  server serves (phase C)
- More terminal engines behind the switcher: ssh. (`git` and `npm` are real
  `msh` commands now)

### `cursor` — the AI pair

AI in the loop of editing: a chat container that knows the workspace, inline
edit proposals you accept by gesture, diffs as first-class containers.
The shell is already multi-view (rings share one live document), which is
exactly the substrate an AI collaborator needs.

### `cursor-agents` — the background workforce

Autonomous agents running against workspaces: kick off a task, swipe away,
come back to a diff. Agent runs as containers — their logs, their diffs,
their approval gates — with the ring as the review queue.

### `n8n` — automation

Workflows as a container kind: triggers, nodes, and connections built by
touch. The gesture shell's spatial model (rings of lanes) maps naturally
onto pipelines; the terminal and git engines become nodes.

### `figma` — design

A canvas container: vector shapes, frames, components, manipulated with the
same two-finger vocabulary the shell already teaches. Design artifacts live
in the workspace next to the code they describe.

### `xcode` — building for the platform

The self-hosting question: how much of building *apps for this phone* can
happen *on* the phone — Swift syntax support, project scaffolding,

3. Models — bound model id, agents inherit, MACHINE.json is a commit

{
  "spec": "kiln-machine/v1",
  "name": "machine",
  "owner": "kiln",

    "shell",

  "isolation": "kiln://kiln/machine.git"

# The Git Tree as a Sealed Machine

**KILN treats every Git tree as its own sealed machine—shell, memory, models, preview domain, ledger.**

ItsNotAI LABS / KILN · 2026 · Working paper KILN-WP-14

## Abstract

A repository on a shared host is a folder with a URL. A repository on KILN is a machine. The computer page already said so. What it did not do, until this drop, is *seal* the five things a machine actually is so they cannot leak across trees: a shell with cwd, env, processes, and ports; memory in six banks; a bound model that agents inherit; a preview domain with an origin that is not the forge; a ledger that is the Merkle of this tree's commits and transactions, not the global chain. Isolation is the repo id. `kiln/kiln` cannot read `kiln/studio`'s banks, cannot share its blob origin, cannot bind a model onto it by accident. A button that opens a terminal on a shared box is not a computer. A Git tree that owns its shell, memory, models, preview domain, and ledger is.

## 1. The object

Call a Git tree T. T has an id `owner/name`, a working set of blobs, a Merkle root, a wallet that may write it. On KILN, T is also a machine M(T) with five facets:

1. **Shell** — kilnsh. cwd, env (`KILN_REPO`, `MODEL`, `DOMAIN`), processes (`init`, `kiln-agentd`, `kiln-memoryd`, `kiln-edged`, `kiln-indexerd`, `kiln-ledgerd`), ports (443 capsule, 7331 MCP, 3000 node, 8000 python, 7840 webgpu, 8443 sealed-cloud). Commands: `ls`, `cat`, `git`, `node`, `python`, `write`, `machine`, `model`, `memory`, `domain`, `ledger`, `seal`. A write is a git commit.
2. **Memory** — six banks scoped to T: working, episodic, semantic, procedural, lattice, folder. Folder memory is the inverted index of T's blobs plus Hilbert cells. The other banks are append-only records on M(T). Search never walks another tree.
3. **Models** — one bound model id on T (`repo.modelId`, written to `MACHINE.json`). Agents on T inherit it. Binding is `updateRepo` plus a commit. The org default is not T's model.
4. **Preview domain** — `owner-name.kiln.app` as the public host, and a blob: URL as the actual origin. The iframe sandbox is `allow-scripts allow-forms` without `allow-same-origin`, so the capsule cannot read the forge's storage. `window.Kiln` is injected with `{repo, isolation, model, domain, ledger}`. Relative assets rewrite to blob URLs from T's files only.
5. **Ledger** — Merkle of T's file root, T's commits, T's transactions. Printed by `ledger`. Not Kiln L1's global height. The global chain still settles `merkle_commit` / `capsule_boot` / `domain_bind`; the machine ledger is the slice that belongs to T, folded to a 20-byte hex root.

M(T) is persisted at `kiln-machines-v1` keyed by `owner/name`, and as `MACHINE.md` / `MACHINE.json` on the tree itself. Refreshing the tab does not mint a new computer. Opening a different tree does not reuse this one.

## 2. Failure modes

### 2.1 Shared box

An in-page Map of shells that dies on refresh is a demo. Two trees that share cwd or env are one machine with two names. The recovered computer stored shells in a module-level `Map` and never wrote them down. Isolation existed only for the lifetime of the tab.

### 2.2 Memory as grep

`memory search` walked T's files. That is folder memory, which is correct and stays. It is not working / episodic / semantic / procedural memory. Those kinds were named in the kernel constitution and never stored. A search on kiln/kiln could not be proven not to include kiln/studio's mailbox because mailboxes were a global agent list filtered after the fact.

### 2.3 Global model

The Models page has Assign. Spawn already fell back to `repo.modelId`. Nothing *bound* the model onto the tree as a constitution, so a visitor who never opened Models ran Grok-4.6 on every computer, including ones that had a different id painted in About. Binding was a UI preference, not a facet of the machine.

### 2.4 Parent-origin preview

The preview iframe used a `data:` URL with `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms allow-same-origin"`. A data URL is opaque, but `allow-same-origin` plus a later `blob:` would collapse to the forge origin. Relative assets did not load. `window.Kiln` was not bound. The host `owner-name.kiln.app` was a string in chrome, not an origin the capsule ran on.

### 2.5 Global ledger

Commits and txs already carried `repoId`. The computer never printed the slice. Merkle on About was the file tree. A machine ledger is the fold of files + commits + txs for T. Without it, "this tree's history" was a filter on a global log.

## 3. Closure

The kernel is `machine-seal.js`. Boot (`kiln-forge.js`) seals every origin tree the kiln account publishes, writes `MACHINE.md` if missing, remembers an episodic boot, ensures the kiln.app domain, seats builder + conductor.

```
GET  /kiln/kiln/computer     five facets + kilnsh
GET  /kiln/kiln/preview      isolated blob origin
     / % machine
     / % model grok-4.5
     / % memory remember episodic bound grok-4.5 on this tree
     / % domain
     / % ledger
     / % seal
```

`seal` is the isolation proof: count of sealed machines, this tree's cwd / banks / bound model / host / ledger root, and a cross-check that no working-bank id, env.KILN_REPO, or domain host is shared with another tree.

`model <id>` calls `bindModel`: `updateRepo({modelId})`, persist M(T), remember procedural, `commitFile MACHINE.json`. Agents spawned after that inherit `repo.modelId` (the store already did). Agents running now see it on the next kernel turn (`agent.modelId || repo.modelId || default`).

Preview calls `isolatePreview(T)`: revoke the previous blob URL for T, map T's files to blob URLs, rewrite relative `src`/`href`, inject `window.Kiln`, create a text/html blob, sandbox without `allow-same-origin`. T′ gets a different URL. The forge origin is not in the capsule's origin.

The MCP tools `kiln_machine`, `kiln_bind_model`, `kiln_remember`, `kiln_ledger` dispatch into the same kernel. `kiln_run` already executed kilnsh; it now understands the new commands because they live in `runOnMachine`.

## 4. What a machine is not

It is not a VM. It is not a Docker container. It is not a Cloudflare isolate. It is a Git tree that owns five facets and can prove they do not leak. Node and Python still execute on the host via `/api/kiln/run` with a tempdir per invocation — that is process isolation for a command, not the machine. The machine is the sealed record plus the origin of the preview plus the bound model plus the ledger slice.

It is not a second website. The original chrome, Models assign, Studio, Wallet, Explore, Marketplace stay. This drop reconstructs the computer, preview, memory, and forge boot, and adds the kernel.

Pickup pin `recovered-20260903` stays immutable. This drop is a new hash-pool branch of `kiln-original`.

    GET /freeze/HEAD.json
    GET /freeze/kiln-original--sealed-machine.json
    GET /papers/machine
    GET /kiln-account.json

Verify with the pool tool against the pin, then against HEAD.

## 5. What this is not

It is not a shared shell. It is not grep dressed as memory. It is not the org default model. It is not a data-URL preview on the parent origin. It is not the global chain with a filter. A Git tree that cannot print `seal` and show a unique host, bound model, bank scope, and ledger root is not a machine yet.

— ItsNotAI LABS, 2026
